title: Meeting Rooms
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every pair versus sorting by start time and checking only adjacent pairs.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of meeting time intervals, where intervals[i] = [start, end], determine if a person could attend all the meetings, i.e., return true if no two meetings overlap, or false otherwise.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Detect ANY overlap among a set of intervals\"","Sort by start time first, then only adjacent pairs need checking"],["A single person attending all meetings","Once sorted, overlap can only occur between a meeting and its immediate predecessor"]]}

blocks.text: Two meetings overlap if one starts before the other ends. Checking every pair directly works but is wasteful; sorting meetings by start time first means any overlap must occur between a meeting and the one immediately before it in this sorted order, since anything ending before that would end even earlier relative to later meetings.

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking a Single Person's Day Planner for Double-Bookings
blocks.text: Picture a day planner listed in the order meetings were scheduled, not necessarily by time. To check for any double-booking, sorting by start time first lets you scan through once, checking only whether each meeting starts before the previous one (in sorted order) has ended.

blocks.caption: After sorting by start time, only adjacent meetings can conflict

blocks.text: Result: false. Meeting [0,30] overlaps with both [5,10] and [15,20], so not all meetings can be attended.

Before checking every pair of meetings, notice that sorting by start time first means any overlap must show up between CONSECUTIVE meetings in that sorted order, since a later-starting meeting could never overlap with an even earlier one without also overlapping its closer neighbor.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Two meetings overlap exactly when one starts before the other ends.

Observation 2: If meetings are sorted by start time, and meeting i does not overlap with meeting i-1 (the immediately preceding one), it cannot overlap with any meeting before i-1 either, since those all start even earlier and end no later than meeting i-1 in the relevant sense for this check.

Observation 3: This means only checking each meeting against its IMMEDIATE predecessor in sorted order (rather than every earlier meeting) is sufficient to detect the FIRST overlap.

Observation 4: A single pass after sorting, checking if the current meeting starts before the previous one's end, is both necessary and sufficient to detect any overlap.
This leads to sorting intervals by start time, then a single pass checking whether each meeting starts before the previous one ends.
Check every pair of meetings directly for overlap.

items: For every pair of meetings (i, j) with i < j, check whether they overlap.
Two meetings overlap if one starts before the other ends.
If any overlapping pair is found, return false; otherwise return true.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Checking every pair directly implements the overlap definition without needing to sort first.
This costs O(n squared), unnecessary once sorting reduces the check to only adjacent pairs.

blocks.text: Limitation: sorting by start time first reduces the check to only adjacent pairs, achieving O(n log n) instead of O(n squared).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every pair is unnecessary: once meetings are sorted by start time, if meeting i does not overlap with its immediate predecessor, it cannot overlap with anything even earlier, since the predecessor already represents the "closest" competing end time.

The single-pass check: after sorting, walk through the meetings once, checking if the current meeting's start is before the previous meeting's end; if so, an overlap is found immediately.

Why this is sufficient: any overlap that exists must appear between some adjacent pair in the sorted order, since overlap is a "local" property once the meetings are ordered by start time.

The core idea: sort by start time, then a single O(n) pass checking only adjacent pairs.
Sort intervals by start time. In a single pass, check if each meeting's start is before the previous meeting's end; if so, return false. If the pass completes without finding an overlap, return true.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Sorted order","Check","Result"],"rows":[["[0,30], [5,10], [15,20]","[5,10] starts (5) before [0,30] ends (30)","overlap found, return false"]]}

blocks.caption: Sort by start time, then a single pass checks only adjacent pairs for overlap

blocks.text: Sorting by start time guarantees that if any overlap exists in the whole set, it must appear between some pair of meetings that are ADJACENT in this sorted order, since overlap is fundamentally about a start time falling before some end time, and the closest preceding end time (from the immediately previous meeting) is the tightest constraint to check. A single pass checking only this adjacent relationship is therefore both necessary and sufficient.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(1) extra (or O(n) if the sort is not in-place).

blocks.text: Meeting Rooms is the foundational interval-overlap-detection problem: sort by start time, then only adjacent pairs need checking, a technique reused throughout interval problems.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "detect any overlap among a set of intervals", think: sort by start time, then check only adjacent pairs.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Checking every pair costs O(n squared) time; sorting then a single pass costs O(n log n) time, both using O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: sort by start time, then check only adjacent pairs for overlap.
Core Idea: after sorting, any overlap must appear between consecutive meetings, so a single pass suffices.
Time: O(n squared) for checking every pair, O(n log n) for sort-then-scan.
Most Important Observation: sorting by start time turns a global overlap check into a local, adjacent-pair check.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, frequently-reused interval technique.
One line memory trick: sort by start; check if each meeting starts before the previous ends.
